If the Grand Trunk Pacific do not earn 3 per cent over and above the working expenses from January 1st, 1923, to December 31st, 1925, they will be under no obligation to pay the government their 3 per cent rent during that same period, and consequently, they will have enjoyed the absolute possession of the road for a period of ten years without disbursing anything. But in this ease, the road will cost the country $244,239,884.28 and the difference between the interest to be paid afterwards at the rate of 3 per cent, and the three and a half per cent interest which we pay, will amount to $908,687 per year and represent a total loss to Canada of $45,433,000 for the term of the lease.
This is the way we own this road which . was to be ours, according to the reiterated promises of the Liberal politicians.
The present generation has made great sacrifices to build this line, and yet that generation will have vanished away before deriving the least advantage from the enormous expense it has incurred, and during fifty years from now on, it must comply with the desire and the will of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company.
The methods resorted to from beginning to end, by the late Administration, in this enterprise, are somewhat curious to examine.
Since the beginning of this debate, a few Liberal members have alluded to Mr. S. N. Parent, the ex-president of the Transcontinental, as being a great lawyer of the city of Quebec. Evidently, those gentlemen do know but very little about Mr. Parent as a lawyer; otherwise they would not have spoken as they have done. True it is that Mr. Parent is a lawyer, but true it is also that he never pleaded a single case and never was considered as a legal light in his province.
It may be well to recall under what circumstances the Liberal Government had entrusted to Mr. S. N. Parent the presidency of the Transcontinental. It was in 1905, and at Quebec, was being written a page of the history of the Liberal party which will surely not be considered as one

of its brightest. In fact, the great majority of the Liberal members of the Quebec Legislature had turned against their Prime Minister, who was the hon. S. N. Parent, and Sir Lomer Gouin and the hon. Adelard Turgeon were leading the movement. Those Liberal members had lost all confidence in the man who, so far, had been their chief. The Liberal party was in full revolt and refused to follow the direction of Mr. S. N. Parent any longer. Shall we ever know the reasons why Mr. Parent's followers had ceased to have confidence in him? However, the public has always been under the impression that the rebels of the time had serious grievances against their chief, and after all, the fact of having lost the confidence of his followers was nothing that could recommend him for such an important position as that of president of the Transcontinental. Setting decorum at defiance, Sir Wilfrid Laurier himself offered to Mr. S. N. Parent, the position of president of the Transcontinental commission, and he then and there declared that he was giving him the most desirable position at the disposal of his Government. Mr. Parent went to work and to understand the methods resorted to in order to build the line from Winnipeg to Moncton, a distance of 1,800 miles, is a real impossibility. That work was divided into twenty-one sections, all of which were very important. It is obvious that the Transcontinental commission, at the time, paid much attention to the big contractors, and in order to make things easier for them, it was decided that the contractors having no fortune, although they might have some talent, should be excluded from the offices of the Transcontinental, and here are the means which were used in order to obtain that result. It was said in the advertisements for tenders which were published in the papers, that those who wished to make a bid should comply with the following conditions:
And we do hereby declare and agree that in case of refusal or failure to execute the said contract with the commissioners, and also to furnish the approved security required, to an amount not exceeding one-third of the estimated total consideration of the contract, for the faithful performance of the said contract, within ten days after the acceptance of this tender the said cheque shall be forfeited to the said com-missionners to liquidate damages for such refusal or failure, and that all contract rights acquired by the acceptance of this tender shall be forfeited.
Those conditions were the surest means of turning out contractors who had no fortune. The commission reserved for itself the right to require from the contractors, as

a deposit, a sum of money equal to the amount of their tender, adding that if the contractor failed to make that deposit, they would have the right to forfeit the cheque representing the deposit, which he would send in with his tender. We shall more readily understand what this meant, when we know that, as to contract No. 1, the *Transcontinental commission reserved for itself the right to require a deposit of $327000, and if the contractor could not make it, the commission had the right to forfeit his $75,000 cheque which he had sent in with his tender, and thus it was with each of the twenty-one contracts. What was the result of such tactics? To have the whole con struction of the Transcontinental let to eleven contractors. And those eleven contractors have become the absolute masters of the former Transcontinental commission and also of the Liberal Government.
What was done by those eleven contractors, the favourites of the former commission? They sold all their contracts and realized profits varying from 10 to 30 per cent, and this, in many a case, before they had touched a shovel or a pick. Owing to the inqualifiable methods used in letting those contracts, these gentlemen have realized profits amounting to millions, and those who sustained losses were the subcontractors, who got no more protection than the public did get from the commission or from the Government.
I shall take this opportunity to submit to the House what has happened, to my personal knowledge, in the district extending eastward from the Quebec bridge, in the counties of Levis, Dorchester, Bellechasse and L'lslet. The main contract in this case had been let to Davis, under conditions which were quite irregular, as I shall prove further on. Davis had sold his contract to the Quebec Contracting Company, but it was thought among the public, generally, that the work was being executed directly by DaviSj and that is the reason why so many persons supplied goods to the Quebec Contracting Company, to the amount of thousands of dollars; they believed that Davis was responsible for the price of those goods. The Quebec Contracting Company was unable to fill the contract which it had got from Davis, and was wound up. This had a disastrous effect in all those counties; many a tradesman has lost important sums of money and the salaries of hundreds of workmen have remained unpaid. It will be noticed, however, as I shall prove a little further on, that in this enterprise, Mr. M.
P. Davis and Mr. J. T. Davis have realized enormous profits.
Another case is that of Messrs. M. Naud and Perreault. These gentlemen did some work on that section of the Transcontinental for which Davis had the contract and which extends westward from the Quebec bridge, a distance of fifty miles. Messrs. Davis had a sub-contract with Roberge and Chag-non, and these latter had let a sub-contract to Naud and Perreault. In filling that subcontract, Naud and Perreault made an excavation, under water, of 2,886 yards of solid rock, for which they were to get 75 cents per yard, whereas the price paid to Davis was $1.50 per yard. Naud gnd Perreault have filled their obligations, but Davis made a final settlement with his sub-contractors Roberge and Chagnon, unknown to Naud and Perreault, with the result that Naud and Perreault have not yet been paid the sum of $2,100 which is due to them since 1908. Roberge and Ohagnon are now in parts unknown and Davis has received big profits, whereas those who should have been paid first have not received anything so far.
The former commission never cared to protect the public, and in many a case the contractors have committed abuses on the properties crossed by the Transcontinental and have laughed at the farmers, at the tradesmen and at their workmen.
I say again that the Transcontinental commission, of which Mr. Parent was president, has shown exceptional kindness to the eleven big contractors with respect to the twenty-one contracts, and that if some detectives of the Burns agency had been called upon to watch what has been going on at the time, as they have done last winter at the Quebec Legislature, surely the detec-taphone would have revealed the true causes of that protection which was bestowed on some all-powerful contractors, and that we would have also an explanation of those fortunes which were amassed in so short a time by certain persons.
I wish to say a few words of what has happened as regards contract No. 8. This contract was for the construction of the Transcontinental on a distance of 150 miles eastward, from the Quebec bridge. As you see, this was a very important contract. The engineers of the Transcontinental say that they have handed to Mr. Parent himself the estimates of the Government for this con. tract before the tenders had been sent in. Did M. P. and J. T. Davis see those estimates after Mr. Parent had got them, in order to prepare their tenders? Here are the facts and I leave it to the House and to the public to draw their conclusions. The esti-

mate handed to Mr. Parent by the engineers contained no price for the wooden piers. Those estimates were remitted to Mr. Parent on the 23rd of January, 1907. The tenders were to be received on the 14th of February, 1907. Mr. Parent was not satisfied with that. It was then the 18th of February, 1907, the tenders had been opened and Mr. Parent knew their contents. He knew that Mr. Davis did not have the lowest tender; but the contract must be awarded to Davis. In order that this might be done, Mr. Parent ordered the chief engineer to stick to the estimate which had been handed to him by this latter on the 23rd of January and which was erroneous, and he had that estimate signed by the chief engineer, Mr. Lumsden, and by the assistant chief engineer, Mr. Macpherson, on the 18th of February, 1907.
As I have said, the tenders had been sent in on the 14th of February, 1907, but the figure was taken off the estimate signed on the 18th of February, 1907 by Lumsden and Macpherson, in such a way as to create the

Had Mr. Parent shown Mr. Davis the estimate which had been handed to him by the chief engineer on the 23rd of January? He says in his deposition that he does not recollect having done so. One thing is certain and it is this: Davis got the contract by means of this estimate, and he could not have got it had the right estimate such as corrected, been taken as a basis.
This contract was awarded to M. P. and J. T. Davis for the price of $5,011,343.50, and up to the 31st December, only 80 per cent of the work had been done, and however, the work called for by this contract should have been completed by the 1st of September, 1908. On the 21st of December Davis had estimates to the amount of $6,341,855.99, or $1,330,609.40 more than implied by his contract.
This contract contained 103 items, and with respect to one only, that is, the item of the filling by train, Davis had estimates for 2,700,000 cubic yards. This item gave Davis 45 cents per yard according to his contract with the Transcontinental commission, and he had sold his contract to a sub-contractor who got 29 cents per cubic yard, which left a net profit of 16 cents per yard for M. P. Davis, who realized $432,000 net profit on this one item.

The work relating to contract No. 16 should have been completed on the 31st of December, 1910, and the work to be done according to contract No. 17 should have: been completed in March, 1911.
Several months after those contract? were signed, Messrs. Davis had not yet begun to work. Of this the president of the Grand Trunk Pacific complained bitterly in a letter addressed to Sir Wilfrid Laurier himself on the 2nd of August, 1909:
My dear Sir Wilfrid,-On the 29th day of October, 1908, the National Transcontinental Railway Commissioners awarded two contracts for the construction of about 204 miles on sections ' D * and * E ' of the National Transcontinental Railway. The first section starting on the west end of Fauquier Brothers' Abitibi contract, in the province of Ontario, about 100 miles west of Cochrane, for a distance of 104.24 miles; the second contract commencing at the termination of the first and joining Fauquier Brothers' contract north of Lake Nipigon, a distance of 100 miles. By the terms of these contracts the work was to commence immediately after the execution of the agreements to be proceeded with continuously and diligently under the personal supervision of the contractor until completed, the date of completion being December 31, 1910.
This work is remote from rail transportation, the closest point being 100 miles west of Cochrane. The prices at which the work was awarded were very high and consequently sufficient to allow contractors to build tote roads or some other means of transportation and getting in supplies so as to immediately commence work. To the best of our knowledge no attempt has been made as yet to open this work, and the indications are that while the work, as before stated, was let at very high prices on account of the difficulties of transportation, it is now the intention of the contractors to haul their material over a portion of the Fauquier Brothers' track work, on which will be completed the present season, say about 50 miles, and haul along right of way to their own section 50 miles distant. This delay will add largely to the profits of the contracts with no commensurate advantage so far as the National Transcontinental railway is concerned, and under the circumstances I will ask that the Government arrange for the cancellation of existing contracts and ask for new bids which can undoubtedly be obtained on very much reduced schedule prices, particularly so if it is known that the contractors will be enabled to haul their material and supplies over such portion of Fauquier Brothers' work as track has been laid up.
Yours very truly,

Mr. Hays also sent a copy of this letter at a later date to Mr. Parent, asking for the cancellation of the contracts, and that new tenders be called for this work. Mr. Parent refused to take any action, and we do not fi^d that any pressure was brought to bear on the contractors to take steps to ensure the early completion of these two oontractr.
The Transcontinental was in duty bound to cancel these two contracts awarded to

Davis, and they had a perfect right to do so under clauses 8 and 20 of the agreements. But Davis was not interefered with and clearly he had elbow room with the commission and more control over the matter than the very men who were bound to protect the public interest. Those contracts awarded to Davis were not canceled, and on September 16th, 1909, they were sold by Davis to O'Brien, O'Gorman and McDougall. These gentlemen agreeing to pay over to M. P. and J. T. Davis 10 per cent of the total cost of the work which was to be done on those two contracts.
The Transcontinental Commission under the control of its president, Mr. Parent, and the Liberal Government itself, sanctioned those two transfers. This handsome transaction, up to the month of October, 1913, had yielded over to Mr. Davis net profits amounting to $740,000, and Mr. Davis made this profit out of the contract without having to turn a spade or risking a cent himself.
These two instances show how truly solicitous the Transcontinental Commission *was for its contractors, and it is on good ground that the investigation commission states in its report that throughout this great national undertaking the late Government sought to encourage extravagance without ever troubling itself about economy.
How are we to account for the Grand Trunk Pacific Company having encouraged such a recklessness and wantonness of expenditure? Simply for this reason, that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company had been awarded five contracts for the construction of ,353 miles of the Transcontinental. On the 31st December, 1911, this company had government estimates amounting to $15,365,000.
The former Transcontinental commission, in its dealing with the Grand Trunk Pacific, exhibited the same extravagance with the other contractors, and should that company have advocated economy, it would have suffered from it, in the carrying out of the five contracts it had been awarded.
The Grand Trunk Pacific Company made enormous profits out of its contracts without taking any risk, by sub-letting all its contracts at a profit of 5 per cent, and on the 31st December, 1912, it had already received net profits amounting to $768,250, accruing from that 5 per cent. The contracts awarded to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company by the Transcontinental Commission were as follows and were carried

out by the contractors whose names appear opposite each contract:
No. 1-50 miles to Corbett and Floresh.
No. 2-39 miles to Toronto Construction Co.
No. 4-67 miles to Toronto Construction Co.
No. 11-46 miles to Macd and O'Brien.
No. 14-15S miles to J. H. Reynolds, Foley, Welsh and Stuart.
None of the guarantees given by the Liberal Government in connection with this undertaking were adhered to, and there is no better way of proving it than by examining each one of the 21 contracts.
Contract No. 1, engineer's estimate of cost, $1,017,051.43; contract awarded to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, the latter undertaking to carry out this contract for the sum of $989,895.90.
The date for the completion of the work was September 1st, 1908, and it was not yet finished in 1912, but on 31st December 1911, the contractors had an estimate of $2,214,311.20.
Contract No. 2, chief engineer's estimate of cost, $326,341; contract awarded to the J. W. McManus Company, for a sum of $289,190.62. The date of completion for this contract was August 1st, 1908, but it was not yet finished in 1912, and the contractors had already estimates for an amount of $587,081.
Contract No. 3, estimate of the cost of construction, $933,137; contract awarded to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, for $767,435. The date of completion of the work was September 1st, 1910, and it was not yet finished in 1912. The contractors had then estimates amounting to $1,042,618.
Contract No. 4, estimate of cost $3,356,389. Contract awarded to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company for $1,898,124. The date of completion of the work was September 1st, 1910, and it was not yet finished in 1912. The contractors had then estimates amounting to $2,805,000.
Contract No. 5, estimate of cost, $2,232,891. Contract awarded to the Willard, Kirchen Co., for $1,646,253. The date of completion of the work was September 1st, 1910, and it was not yet finished in 1912. The contractors had then estimates amounting to $3,023,784.
Contract No. 6, estimate of cost, $1,478,395. Contract awarded to Lyon and White, for $1,385,941. The date of completion of the work was September 1st, 1908, and it was not yet finished in 1912. The contractors had then estimates amounting to $2,409,112.
It would be superfluous to mention each contract, but let it suffice to say that in each contract the conditions as to time and

prices were not complied with by the contractors who benefited thereby, without any consideration for the public interest.
Let us now come to what the old Government did in connection with certain transactions in the city of Quebec.
We have evidence that in those transactions thousands of dollars were paid by the Transcontinental Railway Commission out of sheer favouritism and the Government had received no consideration whatever for the sums thus paid by them. I am referring to Mr. Bergevin's transactions. One Adolphe Chevalier had a dock-yard in the city of Quebec, which was located on a piece of ground belonging to the Duchess of Bassano. Chevalier occupied that piece of ground under a lease which was to expire on the 30th April, 1912. He had been advised that his lease could not be renewed after that date. Mr. Raoul Bergevin, a close friend of the hon. S. N. Parent, who was well aware that Chevalier would have to remove his graving-dock on the 1st of May, 1912, offered to buy his rights for the balance of his lease for the sum of $4,000. This took place in August, 1911, a few week's before the general election. Bergevin told Chevalier that he was buyer for the Transcontinental and that he would give him this $4,000 for the balance of his lease provided Chevalier promised him not to work for the Conservative candidate in the division of Quebec West. That Bergevin was aware that the lease was to expire on the 30th April, 1912, is shown by Bergevin's evidence before the Investigating Commission, (page 575) which is as follows:
Q. But his right was over on the 30th April?-A. Yes.
Q. You knew that?-A. Yes, and that was in September.
Q. And he was to keep possession?-A Until the 1st of May.
Q. Then he would have to get out anyway? -A. Yes.
Being well aware of the fact, Bergevin paid over to Chevalier $4,000, and Chevalier remained in possession of the graving-dock, the plant, etc., and continued to keep possession of it till the lease was over, and on the 1st of May, 1912, he removed everything himself and remained the owner of it.
There is no doubt that Chevalier himself could have got nothing from the Transcontinental Commission, but Bergevin sold to the latter for $4,250, absolutely nothing, and we have the evidence of Mr. Bergevin himself, page 617 of the report, which is as follows.
Q. You did not own the Bassin de Radoub?- A. No, only the right to the 1st of May.
Q. You knew quite well you did not own that Bassin de Radoub?-A. Yes, I did not buy any property.
And yet the deed of sale, dated October 10th, 1911, passed before C. E. Taschereau, notary public of the city of Quebec, says that Bergevin was the owner of the graving dock, as evidenced by the following extract from the deed of sale:
Whereas the said parties of the other part, for the ends of their railway line, require the demolition of a graving dock belonging to the said party of the one part situate upon the lot number two thousand five hundred and twenty-five (2525) on the official plan and book of reference of the cadastre for Champlain Ward, in the city of Quebec, which is the property of the said R. R. Bergevin, he having purchased it from Adolphe Chevalier, by deed of the twenty-sixth day of August, 1911, before Jos. Allaire, N.P.
There is no doubt that this clause was inserted in the deed, in order to have people believe that Bergevin was the actual owner of the graving dock, and yet Mr. Parent who is a lawyer and Mr. Taschereau who is a notary public had before them when they passed that deed, the notarial deed passed between Chevalier and . Bergevin, on the 20th August 1911, before notary Allaire.
Would the hon. gentleman allow me to tell him that what he has just stated shows that Bergevin was the owner of the property?
Mr. Speaker, I have stated that the Duchess of Bassano was the owner of that property.

What does
he sell?

Nothing, absolutely nothing, as will be seen by exhibits 35 and 36 of the report,
But there is another most serious feature to be pointed out in this transaction. Mr. Parent tells us that he resigned his position as president of the Transcontinental Railway Commission on the 6th October, 1911, and yet it was by an authentic deed passed before notary Taschereau, on the 10th October, 1911, (exhibit No. 36) that he undertook, on behalf of the Transcontinental Railway Commission, to give Mr. Raoul Bergevin $4,000 for nothing.
Bergevin states that he really made that transaction with Mr. Parent himself as shown by his evidence, page 576 of the report:
Q. With whom did you make it?-A. Mr. Parent.

Q. He is a lawyer?-A. Yes.
Q. And a very distinguished lawyer?-A. I had to pass that before the notary, Taschereau.
Q And you made the bargain with Mr. Parent himself?-A. Yes.
Let . us now review the transaction made by Mr. Parent and Mr. Bergevin in connection with the Martineau ice-house, (exhibits 32 and 33 of the report). Mr. Bergevin tells us again that he made that transaction with Mr. Parent, on the 11th August, 1911. Bergevin bought an ice-house from Martineau for $2,000; and here again he took good care to tell Martineau that he should abstain from working against the Liberal candidate in the division of Quebec West,
On the 30th September, 1911, after the general election was over and a few days before Mr. Parent resigned his position as president of the Transcontinental Railway Commission, Bergevin sold this ice-house to the Commission by a deed signed by Mr. Parent, for 53,700. Within the space of one month, that ice-house had increased $1,700 in value. There is no doubt that Martineau himself could not have got a single cent from the Transcontinental Commission for this ice-house; but it was quite a different case with Mr. Bergevin who was then doing campaign work in the county of Montmorency, as he himself states, for the son of the president of the Transcontinental Commission, who was then running in that constituency as a Liberal candidate. The hon. member for South-ReiHrew (Mr. Graham) has denounced in this House the change made by this Government in the site of the Transcontinental shops which the old Administration had decided to build at Cap Rouge, about eight miles from Quebec. A few political friends of the old Administration having heard that the Transcontinental shops were to be built at Cap Rouge had bought a considerable tract of land in that locality, with a view to making a most profitable speculation. But then you should have seen- how they raged and fussed when it was decided that the shops were to be built at Saint-Malo, instead of being built at Gap Rouge, and one of those speculators even went to the length of saying that he would spend $25,000 to defeat Napoleon Drouin, the mayor of the city of Quebec, because he had approved of the project of building the shops at Saint-Malo.

(translation) Would the hon. gentleman allow me to put a question? Could the hon. gentleman name the men who were to derive such enormous benefits [M~. Sevigny.]
from the transactions he has just referred to?

Yes. In answer to my hon. friend, let me tell him that I was referring to Mr. Amyot, a legislative councillor and the owner of a large tract of land at Cap Rouge. When he heard that this gentleman had decided to build the Transcontinental shops at Saint-Malo, and that the mayor of Quebec, Mr. Drouin, had approved of it, he stated that he would spend $25,000 to defeat Mr. Drouii. at the next contest for the mayoralty.

(translation) I named Mr. Amyot.

speechtext: I do not see any point of order; it is merely a question that the honourable member is putting to the member for Dorchester.

Evidently there is no point of order.
The old Government had decided to build the shops at Cap Rouge. I stated that certain speculators had bought land at Cap Rouge with a view to making money thereby, seeing that the Liberal Government had decided to construct the Transcontinental shops there, and when finally it had been desired to buy a site at Saint Malo with a view to building those shops there, these same speculators, when they realized that they could reap the profits they were in hopes of deriving from their property at Cap Rouge, uttered threatening words, among others against Mayor Drouin, as I said a little while ago.
They have also found fault with the Gov-ernmeht because they had decided to build the union station on the Champlain market site. Yet, this decision has met with popular approval in the city of Quebec, because the Champlain market site had

been forced upon the city of Quebec and against the will of the citizens in general, with the exception of a few speculators who had bought all the properties in that quarter, for which the Government would have had to pay exorbitant prices, had the station been built on the Champlain market site.
How strange to hear our opponents finding fault with what the Government is doing for the city of Quebec, when everybody knows that, during theii long lease of power of fifteen years, they never troubled themselves about the interests of our city.
In the city of Quebec, friends of the old Government have succeeded in making considerable money, and particularly the office of Taschereau, Roy, Cannon and Parent. On the 2nd October, 1911, after the downfall of the Liberal party, Mr. L. A. Cannon applied to the Exchequer Court at Ottawa, for 99 warrants in possession for the Transcontinental Commission on all the properties situated in lower-town between the Champlain market site and Cap Blanc, and yet it was already a matter of public notoriety that this Government would not carry out the project of the Liberal party in that regard. Mr. Cannon succeeded in making a few thousand dollars which were paid to him by the Transcontinental Commission, and this shows that before resigning his position, Mr. Parent had unduly favoured his political friends, without troubling himself in the least about the public interest which he was bound to safeguard.
Mr. Speaker, one could make endless speeches and weary himself out denouncing all the scandals perpetrated by the old Administration in the building of the Transcontinental.
In conclusion, let me tell the House that the Liberal party went to the people in 1908 with the slogan: ' Let Laurier finish his work.' The Transcontinental had been decided upon by the Liberal party in 1903, and Sir Wilfrid Laurier then said that time would not wait, and that there was no opportunity for pausing and deliberating, before taking action.
He then told the people of Canada: ' Let us hurry up and build the Transcontinental, in order to keep the trade from the west for our Canadian ports, and if we neglect to construct that line now, we shall soon see our western traffic diverted to the United States.' A few years later, when the country had spent hundreds of millions of dollars, in defiance of the promises made to the public, for the construction of that railway,
the same Liberal party came down and told the people that they must approve of the reciprocity treaty entered into with the United States, and by the very fact they were asking the people of Canada and particularly the western provinces to send their products to the United States and to American ports. There was a gross discrepancy between what the Liberal party had promised us in 1903 and what they proposed to us in 1911, and the people of this country refused to approve of such inconsistency and that is why on the 21st September, 1911, they made up their minds that the Liberals had governed the country long enough. The Liberal party wanted to construct the Transcontinental as a testimonial to their leader, without troubling themselves about the interests of the country, forgetful of the fact that men may come and men may go but the country goes on forever. This Transcontinental undertaking such as carried out by the Liberal party shall stand as a monument to the Liberal party in the future, but the record shall never be a credit to that party.

ARTHUR LACHANCE (Quebec Centre) (Translation) Mr. Speaker, the House, I presume, does not expect me to follow the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, through the field which he has thought fit to cover. My hon. friend from Dorchester has been proceeding by innuendos with regard to men who have been held in the highest esteem and have enjoyed the full confidence of their fellow countrymen. To mention only one name, the Hon. S. N. Parent upon whom my hon. friend has tried to cast suspicion as to his integrity in the administration of the Intercolonial, is so much above those attacks that it would be a needless task to repel those attacks, because public opinion has already undertaken to refute them. For fourteen years, Mr. Parent has enjoyed the confidence of the rate payers of the city of Quebec; moreover, for eight or ten years, he has been a Crown Minister and even Prime Minister of the province of Quebec, and after so many years passed by Mr. Parent in the public life of this country, no one has yet been able to point out a single instance in which he has been guilty of a breach of the laws of honour and integrity in the discharge of his official duties. Such is my answer to the remarks of the hon. member for Dorchester, and to the speech which his frame of mind has inspired him to make.
For my part neither in public life nor in private life have I ever made it a practice to proceed by innuendos. This course I

In reply to the insinuations of my hon. friend from Dorchester who would fool people into believing that the transaction in question was engineered with a view to getting money for replenishing the exchequer of the Liberal party, although he has refrained from so saying in so many words, I shall take Mr. Bergevin's affidavit and under the circumstances such a solemn declaration should carry more weight than the groundless insinuations resorted to by the hon. gentleman, in his endeavour to cast odium on the Liberal party.

When the Hon. Mr. Parent was examined before the investigating commissioners, Mr. Staunton and Mr. Gutelius, he also denied under oath having, either directly or indirectly, received any money from Mr. Bergevin, and that the contract was a bona fide contract and that he believed that Mr. Bergevin had never subscribed any money for the election.
I need not dwell any further on that affidavit which absolutely sets at naught the laboured argument of the hon. member for Dorchester.
I now come back to the main subject matter and I wish to point out under which conditions and circumstances took place the investigation held by Mr. Gutelius and Mr. Staunton and the report made by them, as also the positions taken by the different political parties in Canada on that matter. In this connection, it may be said that the Transcontinental National Railway is exclusively the work of the Liberal party. From the very outset, when the project was mooted in 1903, the Conservative party opposed it in the House of Commons as outside of this House, and ever since they have never missed any opportunity of showing their hostility.
Upon two different occasions, at the general elections of 1904 and 1908, the people did approve of this undertaking; but our opponents stuck to their guns and maintained their fighting attitude. For a while they entertained the hope of battering in the project, by instigating the Hod-gins investigation, but they were disappointed in their hopes and their investigation proved to be a flash in the pan. Such was the frame of mind of the Conservative party when they came into power, after the general election of September 21st, 1911.
From time immemorial the Conservative party have had a political ally in the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Now this tried and unwearied friend saw in the Transcontinental a work which was indebted for its existence to a strictly Liberal initative, a most formidable competitor, owing to the immense superiority of the latter, resulting from its hauling power and the working facilities of the line, a superiority which has no equal throughout the American continent and gave it the undisputed control over the traffic in the districts accommodated by it.
Then or never was the time for the allies to pledge, acording to an antique and solemn custom, in an unmistakable manner, their friendship, and could there be found a more convincing pledge than handing over to the tender mercies of the unkind mother the young giant, so that she might crush the life out of him? That is why the Conservative Government hastened to give up their property, that is to say, the eastern section of the road from Winnipeg to Moncton to the discretion of Mr. Leonard and Mr. Gutelius the latter having been, up to then, in the service of the Canadian Pacific Company, and the former having been in the employ of the same company for many year5'. As there was an obstacle in the way, I mean the composition of the Transcontinental Commission, the Government did away with it and as there remained another impediment, I mean the superintendence, inspection and acceptance of the works of the eastern section by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, the Government ignored that difficulty by dispensing with such superintendence, inspection and acceptance, contrary to clause 7 of the contract passed by Parliament in 1903.
Still, as the Government wished to put public opinion on the wrong scent, and draw a red herring across the track, as they wished to find some kind of pretense for mutilating the Transcontinental, as they intended to do,, we have had, consequently, the investigation and the report of Mr. Gutelius and Mr. Staunton, a report adorned with digressions and so exaggerated that from its every page oozes out the constant thought, the deliberate endeavour of finding against the whole world crimes and criminals as also the greediness of salaried commissioners who are anxious to justify the $65 daily remuneration paid to them by the Government for running down and disparaging a national undertaking.
All the same, notwithstanding the warmth displayed by the investigators, what a disappointment this report has proved for the Government! What was to be done? Where there is nothing Csesar loses his rights, and where there is no evil the devil himself is powerless. I say it again, what a disappointment! For, our public undertakings have always admitted of a special meaning for our political opponents: the Pacific scandal in 1873, the Quebec harbour scandal in 1889, the Curran bridge scandal and how many others were impressed in their memory with glistening

remarks in reference to the address in answer to the speech from the Throne: I quote his words:
Now, Sir, about what my hon. friend said for the port of Quebec. Whilst I said let us do what is right for the port of Montreal, I say, at the same time, Providence has given us in Quebec one of the finest ports to be found in the world. But this port has not been equipped so far. Though the city of Quebec has been represented for years by members of the Liberal party in this House, there is not to-day- there was not before we came into power-[DOT] accommodation of berths for more than three ships in the great port of Quebec.
In other words, once more, the Liberal Government since 1896 has not done anything for the harbour and the city of Quebec. Such a statement presupposes a great deal of audacity and very little truthfulness, and no one will trust its sincerity. Who do you expect will he made to believe that the falling off of ocean shipments within the last fifteen or twenty years is due to lack of accommodation? Hon. gentlemen opposite know as well as we do that the only cause is the insufficiency of ocean freight, whether outgoing or incoming, which Quebec supplies, so much so that steamship companies, rather than have their ships stop to load or unload such freight, find it more to their advantage to ship it direct to Montreal and thence to have whatever is needed in Quebec sent back at their expense. The hon. Postmaster General is well aware of the fact, how many a time has the board of trade, and even the city council, strongly protested against that practice and insisted that the freight destined to Quebec firms should be unloaded on the way up. But all was in vain, the answer was always invariably the same: cargoes outgoing or incoming are not important enough.
Moreover, the hon. Postmaster General has himself given another reason besides the lack of accommodation. In the annual report of the council of the board of trade for the year 1913, at page 50, I find a summary of the meeting of April 16, 1913, where reference is made to two letters of the hon. Mr. Pelletier, one relative to the mail service, which is of no practical interest to us just now, and the other concerning the freight question. The views attributed to him in the latter connection are as follows :
The minister expresses the opinion that it is important to clear up the question of the cost of labour at Quebec, which according to the companies' contention, is from 65 to 70 per cent higher than in Montreal. That accounts for the freight being shipped to Montreal thence to be forwarded back here by rail. The

minister thinks it would be a good thing if the Harbour Commission undertook the unloading of the ships having their landing port here at a rate per ton on a par with that exacted from the companies in Montreal.
So that, according to the hon. minister, that wicked Laurier Government is alone responsible. As regards proofs of the zeal of the Liberal' Administration for the welfare of the port of Quebec, our opponents have had them constantly under their eyes since 1896 and have been in a position to record day by day its unmistakable manifestations. They surely must have noticed that the breakwater was extended over thousands of feet, at an expenditure of $2,500,000. That extension has rendered possible for the last five or six years the unloading at one time there of three of the largest of the great modern steamships. How is it that only one company practically made use of that wharf by bringing a steamship there every fortnight? There was nothing to prevent any other company from having its ships land at that point; why did they not take advantage of the opportunity if not solely on account of lack of traffic. Thinking people are aware of those facts, and hon. gentlemen opposite are wasting their time trying to have them view things otherwise than in their true light. That which accounts for the lack of traffic at that port, is the isolation of Quebec, especially during the winter season, from all the large railway and trade distributing centres. What would have been the use of the most improved plant and facilities as long as we remained unable to supply sufficient traffic to induce shipping companies to have their boats stop over at our port? That is j.ust the very point in connection with which the Government endeavoured to help us.
The building of the Quebec bridge originally had no other object. That is another undertaking which the hon. Postmaster General apparently knows nothing of, an undertaking the cost of which was estimated originally at five or six millions, put at the disposal of the Quebec harbour. When the bridge company was formed, the building of the Transcontinental was not yet being considered; that bridge had then as its main object to afford an entrance into the city of all the railways along the south shore: the Intercolonial, the Grand Trunk, the Quebec Central, the Delaware and Hudson and several other minor lines running inland and having their terminals at Levis over one or the other of these lines.
I do not wish to provoke reprisals. But,

since our opponents are constantly repeating that the Liberal Government has not done anything for Quebec, I shall answer that we can proudly compare in that respect the action of the Liberal Administration with that of the Conservative Government from 1878 to 1896.
A single contract is found to the credit of the latter, the Louise Basin and pier, at a cost of about two million dollars, out of which from seven to eight hundred thousand dollars were fraudulently taken; and everyone knows that it was not to benefit the friends of the Liberal cause, but in favour of the friends of the Conservative cause.
To all accounts was not the construction of the Transcontinental the work par excellence which was to revolutionize the port of Quebec and make it one of the most active in Canada; and that thanks to the Liberal Government who took the adequate legislative measures to make it the principal terminal of that line? Then, if the Transcontinental is an accomplished fact the citizens of Canada, and particularly those of Quebec, surely owe no gratitude to the Conservative party for it; have not the Tories sufficiently fought against this enterprise in this House as well as on the public platform; have they not denounced it during the general elections of 1904 and 1908; but the electors, better advised and with better intent, marched on, and now congratulate themselves that this road has become an urgent need of this country. Moreover the antithesis is most amusing; it is really pleasant to see our adversaries take so much pains in trying to force upon the Quebec people the belief that the Conservative party is the saviour of our harbour exactly because of the works performed to implement it, and which are a necessary consequence of the Transcontinental. Would anything be said of these stations, these elevators, these warehouses, these docks, etc., were it not for this line?
Nevertheless, one feels that the present Government have a grud*; against this Transcontinental; the Hon. the Minister of Finance gave' it the cold shoulder last year in a speech in this House-perhaps in the Budget speech-and it was only unwillingly that they accepted the financial obligations deriving from it. He almost blamed it on the Liberal party for having placed this strong enterprise on the shoulders-weak it is true-of the Conservative party; I understand these complaints by comparing the vigorous new performer and the peevish purveyor that the Tory party is towards him. From that state of mind, the hon.
the Postmaser General, although a Quebecker, has not escaped, and we had the counterpart of it, in Quebec, in the decisions which he took with the hon. the Minister of Railways and canals and Mr. Leonard.
They evidently chose to destroy the logic of the whole plans of the Transcontinental. Thus it was logical to locate the shops near the road at Cap Rouge, a point where all the rolling stock must pass from Prince Rupert to Moncton, to build the line along the river in order to have an independent and free circulation, to erect the elevators, stations, warehouses, freight yards at the Champlain market and vicinity, up towards Wolf's Cove and Lampson's Cove; all of which would have been bordered by deepwater wharfs which could have been lengthened at will to thousands of feet according to the growth of traffic. Everything harmonizes in this unity; the Transcontinental is at home, in furniture of its own as we say in law, having exclusive control of its line and terminals and being in direct and immediate communication with oceanic navigation through deep water docks. Anybody can appreciate the strong advantages of such an organization without being an engineer. I will incidentally quote Mr. A. Allan's opinion, who said, in connection with the docks owned by his company near Champlain market:
'I deeply regret,' stated M.. .a.. Allan, ' to be compelled to leave such a fine site which ought in reality to he the center of oceanic trade of the harbour from the standpoint of navigation.
' This site,' added Mr. Allan, ' offered to steamers facilities that are not for the present met with anywhere else, and which the breakwater will never offer later.*
It is then natural that the construction commission guided by those engineers and the advice of the railroad shipping companies, and representatives of all shipping interests should have accepted this enterprise and that the Liberal Government should also have approved it, with the satisfaction, furthermore, of seeing the Board of Trade and the city council of Quebec then and now concur in these views. In fact, in the annual report of the council of the Quebec Board of Trade for 1913, I find a summary of the meeting held on January 30th, 1914; the chairman, Mr. W. A. Marsh, makes therein a review of the year's customs, and I read the following words on pages 10 and 11: The change of government at Ottawa some sixteen months ago brought about a change of plans as to the terminals of this railway, and it is now proposed to have a union passenger

Quebec. Strangely enough, the true reason for this decree is not given. Why this mystery? Modifications to plans are alleged; two years were not needed to change the site of the station and shops; well, that is the only visible result of that slow and equivocal gestation; beyond that there is nothing at all. The last rail between Cochrane and Quebec was laid in November, 1913; this being the case, freight trains oould arrive from the West at Quebec when navigation opened. But there is absolutely nothing there to receive them. The national object of this line is above all to give an opening to the western products, and for the present, and for a long time to come the principal product of exploitation will be grain; henceforth the first facilities needed are elevators and docks to store and ship it. Where are the docks and where are the elevators? Absolutely nothing. But, in fact, the Harbour Board have erected an elevator on the Louise pier; but there is no water there at low tide and it will require years of dredging to reach a depth of from thirty to forty feet. Nevertheless the Transcontinental has no line in the city or outside to reach there; such is the real position, which no one can gainsay.

After recess Mr. Lachance resumed the debate and said:

When you left the
chair at six o'clock, I was speaking of the absolute lack of accommodation at Quebec for the traffic of the Transcontinental, of the trains which could come to us at the opening of navigation, towards the end of April or the beginning of May, and I was recalling to memory the campaign waged by the press of the Conservative party before 1911, against the then Liberal Government, who, they claim, jeopardized the interests of the

City and port of Quebec by the slowness of the terminal works.
Amongst the newspapers patronized by the present Government which gainel distinction in this campaign, I could mention i'Evenement and the Chronicle. Previous to 1911, both dailies denounced the supposed inaction of the then Administration with reference to the terminals; what censure should they not carry against the present Administration, who let two years elapse without a remedy? It must then be that they were not late, if the masters of to-day in Ottawa look placidly on the running out of months and years without raising a finger, even if they claim, however, that-they do not jeopardize the interests of Quebec.
How can one explain the somnolence of the present Government in the face of so disastrous a situation obtaining in our city, if it is not that this apathy is voluntary; and then for what object? Is it to make out of Quebec a secondary terminal which will receive but a small share of the western traffic, or even have to be satisfied with local traffic only? Numerous facts authorize us to conclude so; the most serious and the most peremptory is the scamping of the Transcontinental between Cochrane and Quebec, a scamping which, if not remedied at once, will necessarily reduce that part of the line to a purely local railroad between the two cities. Yes, in the face of the change in grades we must conclude that our lot will result in costly and almost useless buildings that will have served to lead us astray and to meduse us during the time required to plot our ruin and destroy our supreme hope.
In 1903, the Laurier Government had the construction of the Transcontinental voted by Parliament; the contracts stipulated that the western division from Winnipeg to Prince Rupert would be built by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company and the eastern section from Winnipeg to Moncton by Canada. This latter section was to be then operated by the company in consideration of a rent of three per cent of the cost of that eastern section, the lease being for fifty years. It was also decided to at once organize a perfect line able to give- the greatest hauling capacity and the greatest operating facilities that modern civil engineering could produce. And why? Because the progress of the West was so rapid that it would give to that new line at its very inception the full quantity of freight that it would be able to haul.

It is then evident that the most important point was to secure the greatest possible uniformity of level on the whole line. In order to realize this, the engineers fixed the maximum of eastward grades to four-tenths of one per cent or twenty-one feet per mile of rail, and the westward grades to five-tenths of one per cent, or twenty-six feet per mile; and subsequently they brought the latter to six-tenths of one per cent, or thirty-one feet per mile; but it must be remarked that these grades were only to be used where it would be impossible to avoid them, the constant preoccupation being to build a road of uniform level wherever it was feasible.
Such were the instructions given by the chief engineers to their assistants and upon which the line was organized up to 1911.
Owing to these measures, a locomotive could haul at least double the freight weight that she could have hauled on the other lines then existing in Canada and even in the Americas. The highest authorities have given their opinion on that point. Thus Mr. Elliott Cooper, president of the Civil Engineers Institute, of London, wrote on November 5th, 1912, speaking of these twenty-one feet per mile grades as follows:
On the Grand Trunk Pacific, the standard 2,000 ton freight train can be hauled without assistance from Winnipeg to Prince Arthur by a locomotive, the hauling power of this locomotive thus being four times above that of the Great Northern, Northern Pacific and Union Pacific locomotives, and five times superior to those of the Sante Fe, and seven times superior to those of the Canadian Pacific.
Mr. Leonard, speaking on the same subject at a banquet tendered to him upon his appointment to the Construction Commission, expressed an opinion similar to that of Cooper:
It is not easy to say what the completion of that [DOT] line to Moncton will cost; but most *of the works are under construction, apart from 400 or 500 miles between Cochrane and Quebec. The Quebec bridge which, when finished, will be the greatest in the world, will absorb 48,000 tons of steel, and its construction will take five or six years. Eastward, our line has a 0:4 grade, and a locomotive can haul 1,600 tons, whereas on other roads where there is a 1:0 p.c. grade locomotives can only haul 800 tons.
I can quote on the same question the opinion of Mr. Macpherson, to-day Mr. Leonard's assistant, and previously assistant to the chief engineer of the building commission. On June the 2nd, 1909, he spoke before the British Association for the Progress of Science and said:
The distance of the Transcontinental road will be 1,351 miles from Winnipeg to Quebec and as the maximum of the grade for eastbound trains is 21.12 feet per mile, with allowance for curving, tbe most powerful engine built to-day, the Mallet Articulated Compound, of which an excellent description is given in tbe Railway Age Gazette of April 30, 1909, can haul a dead weight of 4,200 tons behind the tender on that grade.	.
Assuming that the tare is 33J p. 100 per ton, the net paying load would be 2,860 tons, averaging 95,333 bushels of wheat for each train. Supposing the profits of that train to be $4.40 per mile of train, exactly double that of tbe profits realized by the Canadian Pacific on every mile of freight train in 1908, it is seen that the cost per bushel for the whole distance of 1,351 miles between Winnipeg and Quebec, is $4.25. The lowest cost prevailing to the knowledge of the writer from Fort William to Montreal, by way of the lakes, canals and St. Lawrence river, on a distance of 1,216 miles, would equalize 4 :44 cents for 1,350 miles, so that at $4.40 per mile of train, the locomotives above mentioned could haul grain eastward on the Transcontinental, from Winnipeg to Quebec, for 0:19 cents per bushel less than the cheapest water route could carry on the same distance, and at 10 :86 cents a bushel cheaper than the present rail and water route could carry between the two points in question.
Under these conditions, transportation cost for every bushel of wheat was to be reduced by one half of what it has been up to date. Such are the enormous advantages that the Liberal Government wanted to extend to Canada in building this road under the conditions that I have just recalled.
More than any other, the city of Quebec was interested in this uniformity of level. The maximum of those twenty one foot per mile grades had been fixed with the object of assuring the entry of western grain in the harbour.
