The British public was surprised, the warmest friends of Canada were dumbfounded, and on all sides there arose a cry of condemnation and displeasure at a country hitherto pointed out as one of the jewels of the empire, for it was believed that its statesmen had sunk to the level of some of the well-known organiza-

tions which are supposed to flourish in the country to the south of us. The credit of this country,, which had been high in spite of serious attempts on the part of wildcat mining promoters and bogus town-site agents, received a severe setback, so severe indeed that I doubt very much whether it will recover therefrom within the next decade. At. first sight there seemed to be a reason for this dismal state of affairs. The despatches had it that an independent, non-partisan commission had declared that $40,000,000 were wasted, if not stolen, by the members of the late Government. It can be easily understood what a feeling this would produce on the other side where commissions appointed to examine into any question are real commissions' who do their work honestly and conscientiously, and whose members, in many cases, are public spirited enough to make special studies of their subject and to act without any remuneration whatever.
As I have already said, these despatches, purporting to be a report of a commission, were really alarming, but when I knew what I have since learned, that a certain number of newspapers only, and these not altogether unfriendly to the hon. gentlemen opposite, just had access to a half-garbled resume of the famous report and gave it forth to the world before any one had an opportunity of examining the report itself, I began to understand how easily it was to place the matter in the unfavourable light in which it appeared. When I received the report itself, several weeks after, and read it attentively page by page, which I did, I wondered how it was possible for any person, even in the heat of political controversy, to destroy the credit of the country on such grounds and with so little justification.
I say, Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that this has occurred, not for the party to which I belong, for I am sure that the people of Canada will understand the situation, but I am sorry indeed for my country, since in my humble opinion, its reputation and its honour should stand higher even in the minds of politicians than mere party advantage.	.
However, when I recollect the debates in this House in 1903 and the campaign of 1904, I am not surprised at the report brought in by the star chamber commission appointed by the hon. gentlemen opposite. In those days there were some of us who thought that it would be a good thing for this country if a railroad were built through a hitherto somewhat uninhabited and unsettled country in order
to develop for colonization, for empire and for trade the vast areas in the hinterland of Ontario and Quebec. Were I to go through the pages of ' Hansard ', recalling to the minds of Quebec members the attacks which were made on the hinterland of Quebec and even Ontario, the morning sun would be shining through the windows of this House ere I finished. Suffice to say that our Tory friends did not want the eastern section of the road built. They, who flew the flag in 1911 and did not want any truck with the Yankees, wanted a read built through the western section of the country and they would have ignored entirely the other provinces. In days gone by the party, of which these hon. gentlemen are the successors, wanted taxation without representation in the old province of Quebec and in this case they proposed to tax my native province without any possible benefit to the people of that province. I was proud as a representative of the city of Quebec to sit in this House in 1903 when the Grand Old Chieftain of the Liberal party unfolded his scheme for the building of the transcontinental line. He told the House and the country that iit was necessary to build another transcontinental line and that in so doing he was going to render justice and fair play to all portions of the Dominion, and that he would open the valleys of New iBrunswick, and the great hinterlands of Quebec and Ontario wherein would toe found in the future homes, for hundreds and thousands of people. We in the province of Quebec had lived on the shore of the St. Lawrence for a hundred years and this was the first opportunity which had been offered to avail ourselves of the advantages of a national highway binding the east and the west , and which will enable us to open up our great northern country with its enormous resources. A railway traversing a province for a distance of from 900 to 1,000 miles exerts a beneficial influence over a wide area of country. Let us suppose that this influence extends for at least 50 miles on each side of the line; that means that 30,000,000 or 40,000,000 acres of land will come in for agricultural and commercial development. Even if the costhas exceeded the estimate, I ask my fellow members not only from the province of Quebec but from all parts of Canada, if our country is not the gainer by the carrying out of this great enterprise? Is there a man in the province of Quebec who will have the courage to stand np and say that our northern country should not be developed? No man at the present time can estimate

the resources of this hinterland of ours with its enormous water-powers, its great forests, its pulpwood, and its iron deposits, the last named of which will one day, through the process of electricity, be developed to an enormous extent. Indeed, the great St. Maurice valley, through which this road passes, with its valuable iron deposits', will offer formidable competition to the furnaces of Pittsburg. It is not alone our mineral and forest wealth that will he turned to good account in consequence of the construction of this great Transcontinental railway, but in the valley of the Harricanaw we have acres and acres of virgin soil which will in the near future be developed by the younger element of the province of Quebec. The cry to-day is: keep the young men on the farm; grow more products, and thus give the people cheaper food, but to bring about this desirable condition, railway facilities to transport the increased productions must be provided.
At this late hour, I shall not enter into any detailed statement as to the benefits the National Transcontinental railway was intended, when originally designed, to confer on my native city of Quebec, my hon. friend from Quebec Centre (Mr. Lachance) has dwelt at length on that. The hopes of the people of Quebec for a prosperous future were based on the completion of this great railway project with its low grades and high standard, which would enable it to carry cheaply the trade of the West for shipment at our ancient port; but the policy of this Government since it has come to power, in degrading the. character of that road and reducing it from the high standard projected by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, has been a great disappointment to our people who, with reason, fear that the National Transcontinental railway will not prove that great boon originally contemplated.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOSEPH DEMERS (St. Johns and Iberville):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should state at the outset that the admirable address delivered by the hon. member for South Renfrew is such a thorough vindication of the course followed by the former government, in connection with the building of the Transcontinental, as well as such a victorious assertion of the national honour and credit endangered by an outbreak of prejudice unprecedented in the history of this country, that I may rightly be taken to task for recklessly interfering in this debate. Accordingly I intend limiting myself to a few and very brief considerations.

This Government, rightly or wrongly, has resolved to have judgment passed on a measure initiated by the former administration. What kind of a tribunal has been constituted for that purpose? What was the procedure followed, and what weight should be given to the findings of such a tribunal?
The two essential conditions required by justice and fair play, and without which elementary conditions no tribunal is entitled to respect, are in the first place, impartiality on the part of the judges, and the right of all parties to be represented and heard. Have both these requirements, or even one of them, been satisfied?
I put the question, though convinced beforehand that there will not be a single member of this House to answer in the affirmative. Two commissioners or judges have been appointed; one of them, an American citizen at the time of his appointment, was gotten from an institution whose interests were in direct opposition to the policy advocating the construction of a new transcontinental line; from an institution which has always, viewed that scheme unfavourably; from an institution naturally jealous of the high class construction of that road, destined as it is to enter into close competition with it and to prevent it from monopolizing henceforth transportation from east to west and vice versa. And it is from the staff of that institution that a man is selected who will draw over $20,000 a year to make an impartial report. But even that was not enough. A year or even more, previous to the making of that report, the aforesaid commissioner was granted a position which I may call permanent, that of superintendent of the Intercolonial with a salary of $20,000 and then he was instructed to " preach economy." I have not the least doubt, Mr. Speaker, that we will have to show thrift henceforth, after making up our minds to pay such huge salaries.
Let us see if the chairman of that commission is better qualified. A Tory and a recognized partizan, an exponent of his party's policy at elections, in 1908, he made the welkin ring throughout Ontario with his invectives against the building of a national railway, basing his opposition at the time on the same grounds which are alleged to-day in his report; and so imbued with partisan notions, that while exercising his duties as commissioner, he despised the rules of the most elementary decency to the point of descending from his com-

missioner's bench to wage war on the Liberal candidate in South Bruce.
Could the Government in good faith rely on the impartiality of these two men? No one will believe it, and the mere fact of the unfair and ridiculous make-up of this commission detracts largely from the weight of the findings contained in its report, which no one can read without suspicion, a circumstance which facilitates for hon. members on this side the task of answering its charges, as the people throughout the country are not likely to give it greater attention than to any other party machination.
The hon. Solicitor General was wrongly inspiied, indeed, when he thought fit to recall the fact that the former administration, as well, had appointed commissions, namely the Civil Service Commission and the Cassels Commission, for, Mr. Speaker, there is a striking contrast between the policy followed by the former Administration and the policy followed by this Government since the hon. Solicitor General himself was forced to admit that both these commissions comprised men whose political views were not even known. It seems to me the hon. Solicitor General, under the circumstances, weakened his case through sheer indiscretion.
I shall now give further proof in support of my contention, that the Government and the commissioners showed bias and unfairness. The report is dated February 11, 1914. We find that, as a matter of fact, the whole enquiry was closed by the middle of March, 1913, with the exception of the evidence of Mr. M. P. Davis, which was delayed until February 5, 1914. What was the object of that delay, if not to excuse the commissioners' tardiness in reporting, whereby they were enabled to fill the columns of yellow papers and to insinuate and charge, and leave the public under the impression that criminal wastefulness had been indulged in, a wastefulness for which the Liberal party should be held responsible, although that party was afforded no opportunty to vindicate itself. I say that such a course is unworthy of an opponent who wishes to be counted fair.
I shall now refer to an incident which occurred during the speech of the hon. member for South Renfrew. The hon. Solicitor General, whose main characteristic is cleverness, thought fit to interrupt the hon. gentleman from South Renfrew while he was dealing with the question of the Transcontinental shops, and insinuated that the $4,500,000 expended on these
shops were not comprised in the alleged wasteful expenditure of $40,000,000 pointed-out by the commissioners.
Why that? Because the hon. Solicitor General fully felt the force of the argument advanced by the hon. member for South Renfrew and how unassailable was the position of the former Government as regards the Transcona workshops, and he endeavoured to ward off the blow.
Now, either that amount of $4,500,000 is included in the $40,000,000 or it is not. If it is, my hon. friend should not have interposed; if it is not, why does the report devote pages and pages to discussing the matter? Would it be perchance, that it was expected the House would be deceived thereby? But, Sir, I wish to state here that the hon. Solicitor General's interruption has contributed more than anything else to - satisfy me that the sum of $40,000,000 represented by the commissioners as being the minimum amount of useless expenditure, was arrived at arbitrarily and on no sound basis. Having taken the hint, I went to the pains of adding up the various amounts included under the head extravagance, and in spite of all my efforts, I have not succeeded in reaching a higher total than $35,000,000, including that amount of $4,500,000 which I have just mentioned.
So I say the position taken by the hon. member for South Renfrew was sound, well taken, when he discussed the matter on the assumption that this $4,500,000 expended on the Transcona shops was included in the estimate of the useless expenditure.
And after listening to the victorious argument presented by the hon. gentleman from South Renfrew on that point, I say there is no fair-minded man but will say that the findings of the commissioners are at variance with the facts, with the law and with common sense and show conclusively the folly of those who have evolved them.
And while I am dealing with the hon. Solicitor General, I may refer briefly to one of his remarks in reference to the entrance into Winnipeg. He stated, if I understood him well, that as a result of the decision of the former Government, the Canadian Northern had filed in court a claim for damages to the extent of $10,000,000. It must be surmised from this fact that the spot so selected was exceptionally advantageous, and I may add, either the Transcontinental had the right to select that entrance, or it had not such right; if the Transcontinental was entitled to make such selection, how can damages be fairly

claimed? If not, why did they not secure a writ of injunction? I think my hon. friend must have had cases which gave him greater concern than this, and I can only express the hope that this famous Canadian Northern case will not trouble his slumbers.
The hon. Solicitor General referred to the Davis contracts numbers 16 and 17. I do not propose dilating on the merits of this question; I am entirely satisfied with the explanation given by my hon. friends on this side who have preceded me, but I cannot forego drawing attention to the fact that the hon. Solicitor General contended that the contractors in the present instance had demanded and obtained prices from 10 per cent to 100 per cent higher than those granted in connection with other contracts, and that, on account of the difficulties met with in the matter of transportation by those desirous of reaching that part of the line. Then the hon. Solicitor General asserts that the work has been delayed, and that when it was later carried through to completion, the difficulties met with at the time tenders were called for no longer existed, owing to the contracts relating to. sections adjacent to numbers 16 and 17 being completed. The result was that the district was more easily reached and in consequence the contract price, he thought, should have been materially reduced. I think the above is a fair rendering in substance of the remarks made by the hon. Solicitor General. What would be the conclusion if all those statements were true? That Messrs. Davis are far from being the keen business men which they have been represented to us to be. Just think, here is a contract for possibly eight million dollars, the carrying out of which, according to my hon. friend's contention, should yield exorbitant profits, it may be 40, it may be 50, it may be 60 per cent, and the contractors, -who are assumed to be shrewd business men, were willing to hand it over against a payment of 10 per cent, that is less than half the average rate of profits on which contractors figures as a rule.
That strikes one as rather unusual, and leads one to surmise a good many things; for instance, when the hon. Solicitor General states that the contract prices were excessive, there must be some exaggeration; when he contends that the contractors delayed the work, there must have been satisfactory reasons to justify such delays, the commissioners' right to cancel these contracts it is likely was not as clear as the hon. Solicitor General contended, they had no assurance that, by calling for new [Mr. Demers.J
tenders, much lower prices would have been obtained, and the commissioners may have thought that serious results might ensue through further delays; and one sure thing is that the artfulness so profusely displayed by the hon. Solicitor General did not make a very deep impression on me.
I had not intended to answer the remarks made by the hon, member for Dorchester, and what I am about to say is merely in passing. The member for Dorchester, in referring to the former chairman of the Transcontinental commission, endeavoured to minimize the reputation as a business man which he enjoys not only in the province of Quebec, but throughout the whole of the Dominion. He contended that the Government should not have given him such a high post of honour as that of chairman of the Transcontinental commission, because, he said, while he was Prime Minister of the province of Quebec, a group of his followers bolted. If it were laid down as a rule that a political leader, a Prime Minister for example, is no longer worthy of public confidence because a group of his followers attempt to get rid of him, pray, Sir, where would be to-day our Prime Minister, the Eight Hon. Mr. Borden, who, in
1910,	if I well remember had to withstand a memorable revolt which came very near ending in his discomfiture? Had the hon. member for Dorchester been here at the time, he would certainly have abstained to-day from alluding to plots and conspiracies. I may remind him of the old French saw: ' Never mention the rope in the house of the hanged man.'
Then, confidence is apt to fluctuate. The hon. member for Dorchester has more experience in this connection than any of us, and I am acquainted with a goodly number of hon. gentlemen in this House who, in
1911,	had no confidence whatever in the present Prime Minister and who to-day seem to entertain feelings of a very different sort towards him.
Now, I shall revert once more to the famous Staunton-Gutelius report. There is a feature of that report which strikes me particularly as evidence of the nagging and fault-finding spirit which presided over this enquiry. It will be found that in every case where steel works have been put up, the finding of the commissioners is that wood or concrete should have been used; and whenever concrete has been put in, their finding is that either steel or wood was the proper material. When cast iron pipes were put in, concrete, they say, was the thing to use, and so forth; in other

words, it seems as though they had made up their minds to find fault with every thing, and these gentlemen even went so far as to criticize and condemn the very decision of the Canadian people to build a new transcontinental line, as evidenced by the intrusion of a few words casting a slur on the building of that part of the line which runs from Levis to Moncton. I do not wish to concern myself with that_ side issue beyond pointing out the lack of judgment and discrimination of the commissioners who have not seen the propriety of keeping within the bounds assigned to them. But we have no time to lose, and I shall leave the responsibility of that report to the government, as regards the advisability of constructing the line eastward from L6vis, though aware that the electors of Levis, L'Islet, Montmagny, Dorchester and other Quebec and maritime constituencies through which the road runs will at the proper time give vent to their feelings as regards this gross blunder on the part of the commissioners. The people have no longer the right to say what they want before the proposal has been approved by Messrs. Staunton and Gutelius, as a matter of grace on the part of these petty sovereigns.
Reference was made to the original estimates of the line and some made a pretence of being shocked at recalling the estimated cost set down by Mr. Fielding at $61,415,000. But there is no one but knows that this figure is not of Mr. Fielding's own making, and that Mr. Fielding was bound to take the figures given by the government's chief engineer, and that was what he did. The government engineer to prepare that estimate figured on an ordinary railway line, that is having steep grades and temporary works. But the government, supported by the Canadian people, decided to construct a high class road and the result, of course, was to- increase the cost of construction.
It was decided, and rightly so, to build a first class road, for there is no sense in carrying through such a gigantic undertaking and be content with the ordinary requirements. As a simple matter of common sense,'the building of a first class road was in order. It is objected:	Instead of
building permanent works, temporary works, such as pile-work, steep grades, sharp curves, &c., in a word all that goes to make up an inferior road, might have served the purpose until it was known what the traffic would amount to. To my mind such a view is mistaken, in connection with a national undertaking of such importance 143
as this. As far as I can see, it is wholly dependent on the question whether the undertaking is necessary or not. But once that point is decided, the proposal to be content with inferior work and to provide temporary facilities, is not admissible; for if the decision is to build a road, it means that the conclusion arrived at is the undertaking will surely be advantageous to the country, that is to say a success, otherwise such a departure would be unjustifiable.
The Government with the approval of th* people decided to build the Trancontinental. Of course, that was equivalent to deciding in favour of a superior type of construction, the cheaper operation of which would compensate overwhelmingly the difference in cost between a low-grade or average railway and a first class road, and would ensure economy in transportation by allowing the circulation of much heavier train-loads, economy in the shape of reduced expenditure for repairs and maintenance besides the advantages consisting in greater safety and greater speed and everything that attracts traffic.
What are the main criticisms voiced by the commissioners? Properly speaking they are but two.
1st, the road is too good, in other words, too expensive.
2nd, there has been over-classification.
As regards the first of these criticisms it covers about two thirds of the $40,000,000. I shall not go any further into the discussion of this point than I did a moment ago when referring to the necessity of building a first class road; but I may observe that there was no necessity for calling witnesses to show that it costs more to build a first class road than to build an ordinary one. An effort has been made to show that an ordinary road is worth as much as a high grade road, but in spite of the endeavours of the commissioners, they failed to attain their object, so preposterous was it to contend that ' better ' and ' inferior ' are synonymous.
There were mistakes, no doubt; it would have been wonderful if none had been committed in connection with such a vast undertaking; but it will be noticed that this ex parte inquiry has not brought to light, directly or indirectly, the slightest partible of evidence of dishonesty, illwill, neglect of duty or inability on the part of the commission or the engineers. Every difficulty which has cropped up has been discussed. Arbitrators were appointed in a good many cases, in a word nothing that



was likely to ensure honest and fair dealing was left undone.
Such is the outcome of the enquiry, though there was no cross-questioning and despite the particularly adverse conditions, as regards the former administration and the former commission, under which the enquiry was carried on. The great majority of the witnesses heard are still in the employ of this Government. The questions put in some cases are leading in the ftrtreme and put in the witnesses' mouths the very answers they are expected to give; some may be construed as imperative in this regard, and whoever reads the evidence given by the various witnesses cannot help saying to himself that many explanations or developments might have been obtained by cross-questioning the witness, though a pretty clear view of the situation may be had by perusing the volume of exhibits, which, by the way, has not yet been translated into French, or at any rate the French version of which has not yet been distributed.
Then, it appears from the discussion that the commission have carefully recorded every thing that was of a nature to further the object for which the commission was appointed, that is to slander the Liberal party. Comparisons have been instituted to show the excessive cost of certain works as against others on the Canadian Pacific or Canadian Northern lines; but in making these comparisons, no allowance has been made for variations in the situation or the time, or even for dissimilarity in the nature of the work performed.
How explain the discrepancy between the actual cost and the original estimates? We might be content with answering: by the greater difficulty of forecasting results as compared with merely recording them. But I think that such a question should be met with an answer or rather an explanation of a more practical nature, and we provide such explanation by pointing out the difference, as acknowledged by the commissioners themselves, between a first-class road and an ordinary road taken as a basis in the working out of the original estimates. Thus the evidence- shows that the original surveys had not revealed the presence of solid rock over a great extent of the line. Then there are the great difficulties in the way of construction, which it is impossible to prevent or to foresee. Lastly, the increase in the cost of labour and supplies. That is more than enough to show the enormous difference that should be figured on when comparing estimates of 
works previous to their carrying out in 1902 and the cost of these works after completion.
But there is this much to be gathered from the inquiry: the work done"is first class, and the country has the benefit of all that has been done, save in the matter of classification, wherein, according to the commissioners, $3,300,000 were paid to the contractors over and above what they were entitled to owing to over-classification, that is to say, owing to faulty judgment on the part of the engineers, since their honesty cannot be impugned by any one, that no one suspects their good faith, not even the commissioners, and since the great majority of the engineers who made the classification have been retained in the employ of the Transcontinental Commission and are still with them.
After carefully going over the evidence, I have come to the conclusion that nothing, absolutely nothing, can justify the commissioners' finding as to over-classification, and I unhesitatingly declare, that a careful summing up of the evidence would have unerringly led them to a conclusion quite different from that which they reached, and that they should, on the contrary, have stated outright that the classification had been conscientiously effected, from the local engineer up to the chief engineer who was called upon to approve of it finally. That appears from the evidence of Walter Youngman, William G. Brown, Alfred A. Paradis, N. R. Beaudette, Stanley Hawkins, A. O. Bourbonnais, G. A. Buttler, Robertson, O'Leary, Pardee, Holland, Charlton, Bell, Bucke, Timbrell, Dick, Holiday, Ferguson, Black, Mattice, Longley, Porter, Hervey, Baldam, Molesworth, Foss, Dou-cet, McFarlane, Grant, and even Lumsden.
All such proof goes to show that any difficulty arising out of the classification was considered and very often submitted to arbitration, and that no classification was settled on before it had been fairly and conscientiously looked into and recognized as being equitable. Everything was transacted above board and decided after due consideration, and the only occasion for differences of opinion (mere differences of opinion) was the unusual character of the material encountered in the building of that road, the original specifications affording necessarily no guidance as to conditions which could not be foreseen previous to the actual carrying out of the work.
As a result of the discussions, the classification was altered at times in favour of the

contractors and at times in favour of the road.
And if I am to infer, as the uncontra-dieted statement goes, that no final settlement has taken place between the Liberal Government and the contractors, there is nothing to mourn over, and it only remains for this Government to set things right and to apply the remedy when the time comes to effect final settlement. Will they do so? What did they do in the case of contractor McArthur? The arbitrators had-decided that over-classification, in his case amounted to $550,000. Was the settlement effected on that basis? Was the settlement effected at $500,000, or $400,000, or $300,000, or $200,000? No, it was settled at $150,000. That shows, Mr. Speaker, what the zeal of these great preachers of economy amounts to in practice.
Commissioners Staunton and Gutelius personally may in good faith differ from the views of the engineers who are responsible for the classification, but their opinion should not be taken into account, and they should have restricted themselves to the evidence heard; had they done so, it would have been impossible for them to draw such conclusions.
Let us not lose sight of the fact that the construction of that railway was superintended by engineers whom the former commission had reason to believe competent. Let us not lose sight pf the fact that the contracts, as stated in the report itself, have always been granted to the lowest bidder; that the Grand Trunk Pacific was in every case at liberty to submit tenders; that the Grand Trunk Pacific whose interest in cheap construction was greater than any other's since they are bound, after seven years operation, to pay 3 per cent interest on the total cost, had the right to supervise the work, and were represented by their most capable engineers, and that the classification, as it is, was accepted by the chief engineer of the commission, by the chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific and by the arbitrators.
Thus we have the best guarantee that the classification must have been carried out as well as it was possible to carry it out, especially in the absence of any proof of dishonesty or improper interference on the part of any one. Besides, there exists no reason whatever for any one to prefer the opinion of people who never worked on the road, who did not visit these districts at the outset, but only five or six years after the work had been done, to that of honest and respectable men who have themselves wit-143}
nessed the difficulties to be met with in the construction; and I do not think the people who are responsible for that classification could wish for a more conclusive acknowledgment of theirr ability and of their honesty than the fact of their being retained in the employ of this administration. For, Mr. Speaker, one of two things, either these engineers were capable and honest, or they were not; in the latter case, they should not have been retained, and since they ha\ e been so retained we are led to the conclusion that they were deemed honest and capable. It seems to me that this does away with any attempt to find fault with the classification. My conclusion, Mr. Speaker, is that, since no dishonesty can be charged against the commissioners, since the classification was effected with more than ordinary care-even if there had been errors of judgment committed by the engineers in some cases with the result that $3,000,000 had been lost, a gratuitous and unfounded assertion on the part of the commissioners-since it has been demonstrated that the course deemed most advisable was decided upon after due consideration of every aspect of the question, I say, notwithstanding what the commissioners may think, public opinion in Canada as well as abroad will be satisfied that the opprobrium rests entirely with those who endeavoured to show to the world that Canadians are either fools or scoundrels.
I for one, Mr. Speaker, believe that the Government has uselessly thrown avray thousands and thousands of dollars on an inquiry the only object of which apparently was to discredit the Liberal party, and the actual outcome of which has been to strike a blow at Canada's credit on foreign money markets.
The said inquiry will also have as a result to satisfy the whole Dominion that the Government's intention is to kill the Transcontinental by departing from the rule of uniformity in the building of the road between Cochrane and Quebec, in such a way that the whole country will be debarred of the advantages to be derived from the operation of a genuine transcontinental line which its present requirements and its future prospects imperatively demand.
The voice of Toronto may kill the proposed Georgian Bay canal scheme; such a powerful influence may even kill the Transcontinental scheme, but luckily for Canada, the powerful voice of the Canadian people will soon make itself heard and deaden tie clamourings which personal interest draws forth from a certain group.

Mr. Speaker, although it is very
late, I feel that I have a certain responsibility and should say a few words on this important subject. First of all, I want to refer to the remarks of the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) who spoke lart evening. He used the following words::
I was somewhat surprised at the attempt of the hon. gentleman to justify the construction -of the eastern branch of the. Grand Trunk Pacific from Moncton to Quebec. I do not think there is another member in this House who has the temerity to stand up and, in view of the criticisms that have been launched against that branch of the National Transcontinental railway, attempt to defend it at this stage. We have every reputable engineer, connected with either the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Government service condemning that branch of the National Transcontinental railway from Moncton to Quebec.
These are extravagant words, and are not borne out by the facts. So far as I know, no hon. member from New Brunswick or Quebec on the Liberal side of the House has ever uttered one word to show that he has not the utmost faith in the construction of the line between Levis and Moncton. The hon. member for North Ontario went on to read the following question from the evidence of Mr. Lumsden:
Did you make a study of the advisability of constructing a new line through New Brunswick paralleling the Intercolonial railway?
There is an insinuation in that question of something that is not a fact, because it is not true that the National Transcontinental railway parallels the Intercolonial railway. Mr. Lumsden's answer is:
No, I never had any discussion with the ministers about it.
With whom, forsooth, would the bargain be made? Would it be made with the representatives of the Grand Trunk Pacific or with the engineers? I fancy that the owners of the road would be a party to the agreement. I want to draw attention to the unfairness of the next question. Here is a Royal Commissioner who was supposed to learn the facts of the case, to be fair to each side, asking a question and putting the answer in the witness's mouth. The question is as follows:
You would not have recommended it, would you?
Is there a civil court or a criminal court in our land in which a lawyer would be allowed to ask a question in such a manner? The commissioners even went so far that, when they did not get the answer, they suggested-
You are not working with us.

You are not working with us; you are dodging the question. Is that a Royal Commission? I think it has been well called an inquisition. It is a one-sided, party inquisition for a purpose. The present Premier of Canada in his election platform at Halifax some years ago said that he stood for adequate protection. I want to call attention to an action of this same Mr. Lumsden who, at the time to which I have reference, was chief engineer of the Transcontinental railway. Let me refer to a report of the Transcontinental Commission of 1905. I am sorry that it will take up some time to read this, but I think it is very important, in view of the misleading and partisan statements published in the Gutelius-Staunton report and reiterated on the floor of Parliament to be sent broadcast throughout this country, that there should be put on ' Hansard ' at the same time and under the same date the facts as they were represented to the people of Canada in 1905 by this same Mr. Lumsden and by his assistant engineer. Is there any further proof that the Royal Commission, so called, has presented to this country a partial, an incomplete, an unfair report ? They were called upon to do a certain duty and they have done it, they have pointed out to the people of Canada where certain sums could have been saved. I think the sum of $6,000,000 is stated as the amount that could have been saved by the use of momentum grades as against a practically level road. What of it ? I ask, what of it ? I charge that there is not a hint in that report from one cover to the other that any member of the commission, any one of the engineers in the employ of and paid by the Government, dishonestly used for his own benefit, one dollar of public funds; and it is a credit to the Government that $180,000,000 of the public money has been expended and that yet, after an investigation, there is not a hint that one dollar was taken by a servant of the Government unfairly. If that is not creditable I do not know what could be. The report says that so much money could have been saved by degrading the standard of the road, for instance by building the substructure at Quebec partly of wood and partly of cement. Then, it says, so much could have been saved by using wooden trestles instead of solid fill. They say that $40,000,000 have been misspent. They mention these different items but they do not
add up to anything like $40,000,000. Tiie $40,000,000 can only be reached by compounding interest on the amounts. The calculation I have shown will prove to you and to every member of this House that the late Government acted wisely in providing for a road of the highest possible standard.
I am sorry to have to say that this is an unfair report. We all know what the agreement was. The commission have very unfairly represented the object of the railway. They say simply that it was a means to secure cheaper transportation. But this road opens up a new country; by its construction we roll back to the northward the map of Canada. It is a colonization road as well as a road for transportation from the East to the West, and there are advantages accruing to Canada from the construction of this road in the way of new population in the Northland. Many thousands of loyal Canadians will be located along this road. Many are now locating there in Quebec and New Brunswick. I said in my opening remarks that it was unfair for the hon. member for North Ontario to say that this road parallels the Intercolonial railway. We might as well say that all roads running east and west parallel each other. In a sense it is true, but if hon. gentlemen will take the map they will find a difference between the Intercolonial railway and this line; they will observe that it opens up an entirely new section through New Brunswick, a section that probably would not have been opened for the next hundred years if it had not 'been for the fact that this is a part of a through line, because the local trade would not of itself be sufficient to support a railway.
I think I have demonstrated that that report is wilfully partisan, that the commissioners have wilfully omitted things they ought to have put in the report and that they have given an overdrawn picture of other things which they have inserted in their report. They have put answers in the witnesses' mouths, they have been unfair; and if it is wilfully partisan it is misleading, so that the words of the amendment are words that are actually borne out by the facts. Will hon. gentlemen vote against the facts or will they stand up and vote so that it cannot be said to the world at large that the Government of the day have endorsed what hon. gentlemen have said regarding the construction of this railway? Let me put one more thing to you. If there is one thing more than another

that seems to me unfair in this report it is the statement made with regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific on page 24 of the report.
They insinuate that the Grand Trunk Pacific condoned the overbreak, or paying to the contractors more than they had a right to get, because, forsooth, the Grand Trunk Pacific themselves were contractors. Then the report goes on to say that they did not do the work themselves but that they sublet their contracts on the basis of 5 per cent. Thus they insinuate that the Grand Trunk Pacific, for the paltry sum of 5 per cent of any amount alleged to have been paid as overbreak more than should have been allowed by the engineers, acted contrary to the interests of the stockholders of that corporation. Is it worthy, ot unworthy, of the Government of the day to say that about a great corporation like the Grand Trunk Pacific? I think it is a slander on the Grand Trunk Pacific and on the Grand Trunk, the pioneer railway organization of Canada. That is another reason why I say that the amendment is in accordance with the facts and ought to be voted for by every member of this House.
The acting Minister of Railways, in addressing this House on the subject, was most unfair in adding to his statement $42,000,000 ior seven years' interest, as the amount, on the basis of the rental, which the road will have to pay. That is absolutely unfair because every man in this House knows that the Grand Trunk Pacific are to have the Toad for seven years Tent free 'and if you add seven years' interest and they have to pay interest on that amount for 43 years, that they are not receiving seven years' rent free. When the attention of the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) was drawn to that he said that the acting Minister of Railways and Canals was right. I am willing to excuse the Postmaster General because, perhaps, he did not know the facts, but there is no excuse for the acting Minister of Railways and Cana'ls in putting that statement before the country. It was unfair on the part of the royal commission not to show the advantages in the way of operation as against the interest charges. It was unfair not to show that the Grand Trunk Pacific entered into that agreement for 0 -4 per cent and 0-.6 per cent grades. Perhaps I ought not to put it exactly in that way because there is a clause in the report that the Grand Trunk Pacific entered into that agreement for 0.4 per cent and 0.6 per cent grades

on the cost of which they have to pay interest for 43 years. Would the Grand Trunk Pacific wish an undue cost to be added to the 1,800 miles of road in order to cover up an alleged overcharge with respect to the 271 miles for which they themselves had the contract ? It was unfair of the commissioners to endeavour to have witnesses answer the questions of the commission in a way which would not be allowed by any judge in any civil ior criminal court. It was unfair to allege that those in charge of the construction, including the Grand Trunk Pacific, did not consider it desirable or necessary to encourage economy in the construction. The statement of the royal commission in that regard is absolutely without foundation. It is all very well for them to make a statement like that but they have not substantiated it. All they have substantiated is that the railway could have been built for less money by degrading it. In the same way, if you start to build a store, you can lessen the cost by degrading the character of the work. I have read the report through, although I have not read all the evidence, and that is all I can find in it.
I have nothing more to say than that it will give me great pleasure to vote for the amendment. I think the amendment is in accordance with the facts. I am sorry to think that this report has to go broadcast through the country making these unfair insinuations against the Grand Trunk Pacific. It does an injustice to the credit of Canada and to the management of public affairs. I suppose that its object is to do duty before the country. It seems to me that we might place on the title page the words ' adequate protection '. Then, it will do its duty when the election comes on. It will then be said by those who have charge of the election campaign, as the commission say on page 15 that,
' $40,000,000 at least was needlessly expended in the building of this road.' Then some paper, or some supporter of the Government, will take up the cry that $40,000,000 of the people's money has been squandered. Then it will be added to and it will be said that .something worse than that has been done with $40,000,000 of the people's money. Then there will be the story-the money is gone but there is no money for the navy; they refused $35,000,000 to protect the old land. That would not be true if they did say that. It is not true at all because we were willing to give very much more than $35,000,000; we offered it.
